title: Bruxism: Grinding Your Teeth Is the Pits
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss bruxism (teeth grinding and clenching), covering daytime versus nighttime grinding, the cyclical nature of grinding episodes, the high pressure involved, and dental damage such as worn enamel, cracks, and root canals. They review causes including stress, anxiety, dehydration, smoking, heavy drinking, allergies, malocclusion, sleep disturbances, parasitic worm infections, and certain medications, and note the trait may be inherited and more common in women. They discuss TMJ versus TMD, jaw surgery, pillows and sleep position, and children's teeth grinding, which usually fades between ages seven and twelve. Remedies include mouth guards, relaxation, habit breaking, and the Grind Care device sold only in Germany, Denmark and Sweden. The episode ends with a book plug for the Stuff You Should Know book and listener mail correcting an earlier heroin episode about post-acute withdrawal syndrome (PAWS).

entities.name: Stuff You Should Know: An Incomplete Compendium of Mostly Interesting Things

segments.title: Book plug and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck plug the upcoming Stuff You Should Know book and joke about Chuck's teeth grinding. They introduce bruxism and its two main types, daytime and nighttime grinding.

segments.title: Bruxism cycles and force
segments.summary: Bruxism is described as cyclical, occurring in clusters of episodes with rising and falling heart rate and brain activity. Grinding can exert up to 250 pounds per square inch, far more than normal chewing, and wears enamel quickly. The hosts discuss dental consequences such as cracks, fractures, exposed nerves and root canals.

segments.title: Prevalence, stress and causes
segments.summary: The hosts note that bruxism is common and seems to be rising with stress, especially in adults. Grinding is distinguished from clenching, and bruxism is classed as a parafunctional habit. Risk factors include being a woman, smoking, heavy drinking, and dehydration, and the hosts question why the body responds to stress this way.

segments.title: Causes: malocclusion, sleep, parasites and medication
segments.summary: Other causes discussed include sleep disturbances, asymmetric bite (malocclusion) and its treatments such as jaw shortening surgery, parasitic worm infections, allergies, certain psychiatric medications and antidepressants, and sleep apnea. Chuck describes his own bite changes and jaw surgery he considered.

segments.title: Signs, TMJ versus TMD, and sleep pillows
segments.summary: Signs of bruxism include sore jaw, cheek rubbing, and bite marks. The hosts clarify that TMJ is the joint and TMD is the disorder affecting it, with clicking, popping, and pain. They also discuss lockjaw and pillows designed for sleep position and snoring.

segments.title: Children, teething and treatment
segments.summary: Babies often grind during teething, and children commonly grind until about age seven to twelve, when adult teeth come in. Grinding in children can disrupt sleep. Treatments discussed include warm baths, stories, topical analgesics, tongue placement, meditation, reducing caffeine and gum chewing, and breaking habits.

segments.title: Grind Care device and other remedies
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Grind Care device, a headband-style monitor with electrical pulses sold only in Germany, Denmark and Sweden. They also discuss a bitter-tasting or annoying mouth guard insert that punctures to deliver an unpleasant taste.

segments.title: Book plug and tangents
segments.summary: Hosts mention the book again and tell a brief anecdote about a Vegas shirt trip, then transition to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: heroin withdrawal correction
segments.summary: A listener, Jason, a former opiate addict, corrects the earlier heroin episode, noting that acute withdrawal lasting about a week does not equal full recovery and that post-acute withdrawal syndrome (PAWS) and long-term support are needed. Josh and Chuck acknowledge the error.
